questions.question_title: Section 4: Diversion of Income vs Application of Income
questions.question_text: Mr. Bhargava, a leading advocate on corporate law, decided to reduce his practice and to accept briefs only for paying his taxes and making charities with fees received on such briefs. In a particular case, he agreed to appear to defend one company in Supreme Court on the condition that he would be provided with ₹ 5 lacs for a public charitable trust that he would create. He defended the company and was paid the sum by company. He created a trust of that sum by executing a trust deed. Decide whether the amount received by Mr. Bhargava is assessable in his hands as income from profession.
questions.answer_text:
In the instant case, the trust was created by Mr. Bhargava himself out of his professional income. The client did not create the trust. The client did not impose any obligation in the nature of a trust binding on Mr. Bhargava. Thus, there is no diversion of the money to the trust before it became professional income in the hands of Mr. Bhargava. This case is one of application of professional income and not of diversion of income by overriding title.

Therefore, the amount received by Mr. Bhargava is chargeable to tax under the head "Profits and gains of business or profession".

questions.subject: dt
questions.question_title: Section 4: Diversion of Income by Overriding Title vs. Application of Income
questions.question_text: XYZ Ltd. took over the running business of a sole-proprietor by a sale deed. As per the sale deed, XYZ Ltd. undertook to pay overriding charges of ₹ 15,000 p.a. to the wife of the sole-proprietor in addition to the sale consideration. The sale deed also specifically mentioned that the amount was charged on the net profits of XYZ Ltd., who had accepted that obligation as a condition of purchase of the going concern. Is the payment of overriding charges by XYZ Ltd. to the wife of the sole-proprietor in the nature of diversion of income or application of income? Discuss.
questions.answer_text: This issue came up for consideration before the Allahabad High Court in Jit & Pal X-Rays (P.) Ltd. v. CIT (2004) 267 ITR 370 (All). The Allahabad High Court observed that the overriding charge which had been created in favour of the wife of the sole-proprietor was an integral part of the sale deed by which the going concern was transferred to the assessee. The obligation, therefore, was attached to the very source of income i.e. the going concern transferred to the assessee by the sale deed. The sale deed also specifically mentioned that the amount in question was charged on the net profits of the assessee-company and the assessee-company had accepted that obligation as a condition of purchase of the going concern. Hence, it is clearly a case of diversion of income by an overriding charge and not a mere application of income.

questions.subject: dt
questions.question_title: Section 4: Diversion of Income by Overriding Title vs Application of Income
questions.question_text:
MKG Agency is a partnership firm consisting of father and three major sons. The partnership deed provided that after the death of father, the business shall be continued by the sons, subject to the condition that the firm shall pay 20% of the profits to the mother. Father died in March, 2025. In the previous year 2025-26, the reconstituted firm paid ₹ 1 lakh (equivalent to 20% of the profits) to the mother and claimed the amount as deduction from its income.

Examine the correctness of the claim of the firm.
questions.answer_text:
The issue raised in the problem is based on the concept of diversion of income by overriding title, which is well recognised in the income-tax law.

In the instant case, the amount of ₹ 1 lakh, being 20% of profits of the firm, paid to the mother gets diverted at source by the charge created in her favour as per the terms of the partnership deed. Such income does not reach the assessee-firm.

Rather, such income stands diverted to the other person as such other person has a better title on such income than the title of the assessee. The firm might have received the said amount but it so received for and on behalf of the mother, who possesses the overriding title.

Therefore, the amount paid to the mother should be excluded from the income of the firm. This view has been confirmed in CIT vs. Nariman B. Bharucha & Sons (1981) 130 ITR 863 (Bom).

Assume that the company has not exercised option under section 115BAA or 115BAB. [Note - The gross receipts of X Ltd. for the P.Y.2023-24 is ₹ 402 crore]
questions.answer_text:
The tax payable on total income of ₹ 1,01,00,000 of X Ltd. computed @ 32.1% (including surcharge @ 7%) is ₹ 32,42,100.

However, the tax cannot exceed ₹ 31,00,000 (i.e., the tax of ₹ 30,00,000 payable on total income of ₹ 1 crore plus ₹ 1,00,000, being the amount of total income exceeding ₹ 1 crore).

Therefore, the tax payable on ₹ 1,01,00,000 would be ₹ 31,00,000.

The marginal relief is ₹ 1,42,100 (i.e., ₹ 32,42,100 - ₹ 31,00,000).

questions.subject: dt
questions.question_title: Section 2(1A) & 10(1): Definition and Tests of Agricultural Income
questions.question_text: Ankur, the owner of a land situated in Kerala used for growing thereon different types of fruits, paddy, vegetables and flowers, received from Yahoo Movies Ltd., Chennai, ₹ 5 lacs as rent towards the use of this land for shooting of a film. The amount so received was accounted by him in the books as revenue derived from land and claimed to be exempt under section 10(1). He now wants to confirm from you whether the amount has been correctly treated by him as agricultural income.
questions.answer_text: The income received by Mr. Ankur from a filmmaker for allowing them to shoot a film in the agricultural land owned by him is not in the nature of agricultural income because it was neither received by him against the sale of agricultural produce obtained nor for carrying out the normal agricultural operations on the land. The amount paid was only for the purpose of shooting of a film on such land. To claim exemption in respect of agricultural income under section 10(1), the conditions contained in section 2(1A)(a) to (c) have to be first complied with/fulfilled by the assessee. The Madras High Court in case of B. Nagi Reddi v. CIT (2002) 258 ITR 719, following judgment of Apex Court in case of CIT v Raja Benoy Kumar Sahas Roy (1957) 32 ITR 466, has held, on identical facts, that income derived for allowing a shooting of film in agricultural land cannot be treated as agricultural income, as it has no nexus with the land, except that it was carried out on agricultural land.

questions.question_title: Agricultural Income Exceptions & Sikkimese Individual Exemption
questions.question_text:
Examine with reasons, based on the provisions of the Act, as to chargeability of the following receipts to tax:

- **(i)** Rent of ₹ 60,000 charged from tenants occupying houses constructed on the land situated in India and used for agricultural purposes. The tenants, working in the nearby industrial area, occupy these houses for their own residential purposes.

- **(ii)** Income of ₹ 75,000 derived by Anand Nursery from the sale of seedlings grown without carrying out all the basic operations on land.

- **(iii)** Mr. Gaitonde, born and brought up in the State of Sikkim, had a net profit of ₹ 2,25,000 from the business located in Sikkim and interest of ₹ 55,000 on the securities/bonds issued by the Government of Rajasthan.
questions.answer_text:
- **(i)** As per section 10(1), agricultural income is exempt from tax. The meaning and scope of agricultural income is defined in section 2(1A). According to Explanation 2 to section 2(1A), any income derived from any building from the use of such building for any purpose (including letting for residential purposes or for the purpose of any business or profession) other than agriculture shall not be agricultural income.

Therefore, the rent of { 60,000 from letting out of houses constructed on agricultural land for residential purposes of industrial workers shall not be treated as agricultural income by virtue of Explanation 2 to section 2(1A). Hence, such income would be chargeable to tax. Basic Concepts, Tax Rates and Exempt Income eg ee ee

- **(ii)** Explanation 3 to section 2(1A) provides that the income derived from saplings or seedlings grown in a nursery shall be deemed to be agricultural income, whether or not the basic operations were carried out on land.

Accordingly, the income of ₹ 75,000 derived by Anand Nursery from the sale of seedlings grown without carrying out all the basic operations on land shall be treated as agricultural income and exempt from tax under section 10(1).

- **(iii)** Section 10(264AA) exempts the income which accrues or arises to a Sikkimese individual from any source in the State of Sikkim and the income by way of dividend or interest on securities.

Therefore, the income of Mr. Gaitonde from a business located in Sikkim and interest income on the securities/bonds of Government of Rajasthan shall not be subject to tax.

questions.subject: dt
questions.question_title: Section 10(10BC): Exemption of Disaster Compensation
questions.question_text: An amount of ₹ 5 lacs was paid to the parents of Amit by the Government of Chattisgarh as compensation to the aggrieved family, whose only son Amit lost his life in Maoist local bus bomb blast in Dantewada. Examine with reasons, whether the amount of compensation received is chargeable to tax?
questions.answer_text:
As per section 10(10BC), the meaning of "disaster" shall be derived from Disaster Management Act, 2005 which defines disaster to mean a catastrophe, mishap, calamity or grave occurrence in any area, arising from natural or manmade causes, or by accident or negligence. It should have the effect of causing substantial loss of life or human suffering or damage to, and destruction of property, or damage to, or degradation of environment. It should be of such a nature or magnitude to be beyond the coping capacity of the community of the affected area. If, for this reason, any compensation is paid by the Central Government or by a State Government or by a local authority, then, the same will be exempt from tax.

Accordingly, the amount of ₹ 5 lacs received by the parents of deceased Amit from the Government of Chattisgarh for the disaster because of Dantewada bus bomb blast is exempt under section 10(10BC). CHAPTER - 2 Transactions not regarded as Transfer

questions.subject: dt
questions.question_title: Section 47: Transactions Not Regarded as Transfer (Exempted Capital Asset Transfers)
questions.question_text:
In which of the following situations capital gains tax liability does not arise?

- **(i)** Mr. A purchased gold in 1970 for ₹ 25,000. In the P.Y. 2025-26, he gifted it to his son at the time of marriage. Fair market value (FMV) of the gold on the day gift was made was ₹ 1,00,000.

- **(ii)** A house property is purchased by a Hindu undivided family in 1945 for ₹ 20,000. It is given to one of the family members in the P.Y. 2025-26 at the time of partition of the family. FMV on the day of partition was ₹ 12,00,000.

- **(iii)** Mr. B purchased 50 convertible debentures for ₹ 40,000 in 1995 which are converted in to 500 shares worth ₹ 85,000 in November 2025 by the company.
questions.answer_text:
We know that capital gains arise only when we transfer a capital asset. The liability of tax in the situations given above is discussed as follows:

- **(i)** As per the provisions of section 47 (iii), transfer of a capital asset by an individual under a gift is not regarded as transfer for the purpose of capital gains.

Therefore, capital gains tax liability does not arise in the given situation.

- **(ii)** As per the provisions of section 47(i), transfer of a capital asset (being in kind) on the total or partial partition of Hindu undivided family is not regarded as transfer for the purpose of capital gains.

Therefore, capital gains tax liability does not arise in the given situation.

- **(iii)** As per the provisions of section 47(x), transfer by way of conversion of bonds or debentures, debenture stock or deposit certificates in any form of a company into shares or debentures of that company is not regarded as transfer for the purpose of capital gains.

Therefore, capital gains tax liability does not arise in the given situation. TT __ ATR1CA Career Institute (ACI) Capital Gains

questions.question_title: Tax Treatment of Reverse Mortgage Scheme u/s 47(xvi) and 10(43)
questions.question_text: Mr. Abhishek a senior citizen, mortgaged his residential house with a bank, under a notified reverse mortgage scheme. He was getting loan from bank in monthly installments. Mr. Abhishek did not repay the loan on maturity and hence gave possession of the house to the bank, to discharge his loan. How will the treatment of long-term capital gain be on such reverse mortgage transaction?
questions.answer_text:
Section 47(xvi) provides that any transfer of a capital asset in a transaction of reverse mortgage under a scheme made and notified by the Central Government shall not be considered as a transfer for the purpose of capital gain.

Accordingly, the mortgaging of residential house with bank by Mr. Abhishek will not be regarded as a transfer.

Therefore, no capital gain will be charged on such transaction. Further, section 10(43) provides that the amount received by the senior citizen as a loan, either in lump sum or in installment, in a transaction of reverse mortgage would be exempt from income-tax.

Therefore, the monthly installment amounts received by Mr. Abhishek would not be taxable. However, capital gains tax liability would be attracted at the stage of alienation of the mortgaged property by the bank for the purposes of recovering the loan.

questions.question_title: Succession of Sole Proprietorship by Company: Section 47(xiv), Cost under Section 49(1) & Period of Holding under Section 2(42A)
questions.question_text:
Neerja was carrying on the textile business under a proprietorship concern, Neerja Textiles. On 30.12.2025 the business of Neerja Textiles was succeeded by New Look Textile Private Limited and all the assets and liabilities of Neerja Textiles on that date became the assets and liabilities of New Look Textile Private Limited and Neerja was given 52% share in the share capital of the company. No other consideration was given to Neerja on account of this succession. The assets and liabilities of Neerja Textiles transferred to the company include an urban land which was acquired by Neerja on 19.7.2013 for ₹ 9,80,000. The company sold the same on 30.03.2026 for ₹ 16,00,000.

Examine the tax implication of the above-mentioned transaction and compute the income chargeable to tax in such case(s).
questions.answer_text:
Taxability in case of succession of Neerja Textiles by New Look Textile Private Limited As per provisions of section 47(xiv), in case a proprietorship concern is succeeded by a company in the business carried by it and as a result of which any capital asset is transferred to the company, then the same shall not be treated as transfer and will not be chargeable to capital gain tax in case the following conditions are satisfied:

- **(1)** all assets and liabilities of sole proprietary concern becomes asset and liabilities of company.

- **(2)** the shareholding of sole proprietor in company is not less than 50% of total voting power of company and continues to remain as such for a period of 5 years from the date of succession.

- **(3)** the sole proprietor does not receive any consideration or benefit in any form from the company other than by way of allotment of shares in the company. In the present case, all the conditions mentioned above are satisfied therefore, the transfer of capital asset by Neerja Textiles to New Look Textiles Private Limited shall not attract capital gain tax provided Neerja continues to hold 50% or more of voting power of New Look Textiles Private Limited for a minimum period of 5 years.

Taxability in case of transfer of land by New Look Textiles Private Limited As per the provisions of section 49(1) and Explanation 1 to section 2(42A), in case a capital asset is transferred in the circumstances mentioned in section 47(xiv}, the cost of the asset in the hands of the company shall be the cost of the asset in the hands of the sole proprietor.

Consequently, for the determining the period of holding of the asset, the period for which the asset is held by the sole proprietor shall also be considered.

Therefore, in the present case, the urban land shall be a long-term capital asset since it is held for more than 24 months by New Look Textile Private Limited and Neerja Textiles taken together. Cost a nF AIR1iCA Career Institute (ACI) of acquisition of land in the hands of the company shall be ₹ 9,80,000 i.e., the purchase cost of the land in the hands of Neerja.

questions.question_title: Demerger Tax Framework: Section 47 Exemption, Cost Allocation & Section 54F Integration
questions.question_text:
SS(P) Ltd., an Indian company having two undertakings engaged in manufacture of cement and steel, decided to hive off cement division to RV(P) Ltd., an Indian company, by way of demerger. The net worth of SS(P) Ltd. immediately before demerger was ₹ 40 crores. The net book value of assets transferred to RV(P) Ltd. was ₹ 10 crores. The demerger was made in January 2026. In the scheme of demerger, it was fixed that for each equity share of ₹ 10 each (fully paid up) of SS(P) Ltd., two equity shares of ₹ 10 each (fully paid up) were to be issued. One Mr. N.K. held 25,000 equity shares in SS(P) Ltd. which were acquired in financial year 2004-05 for ₹ 6,00,000. Mr. N.K. received 50,000 equity shares from RV(P) Ltd. consequent to demerger in January 2026. He sold all the shares of RV(P) Ltd. for ₹ 8,00,000 in March, 2026. In this background you are requested to answer the following:

- **(i)** Does the transaction of demerger attract any income tax liability in the hands of SS(P) Ltd. and RV(P) Ltd.?

- **(ii)** Compute the capital gain that could arise in hands of Mr. N.K. on receipt of shares of RV(P) Ltd.

- **(iii)** Compute the capital gain that could arise in the hands of Mr. N.K. on sale of shares of RV(P) Ltd.

- **(iv)** Will the sale of shares by Mr. N.K. affect tax benefits availed by SS(P) Ltd. and/or RV(P) Ltd.?

- **(v)** Is Mr.N.K. eligible to avail any tax exemption under any of the provisions of the Income-tax Act, 1961 on the sale of shares of RV(P) Ltd.? If so, mention in brief.
questions.answer_text:
- **(i)** No, the transaction of demerger would not attract any income-tax liability in the hands of SS(P) or RV(P) Ltd.

As per section 47(vib), any transfer in a demerger, of a capital asset, by the demerged company to the resulting company would not be regarded as "transfer" for levy of capital gains tax if the resulting company is an Indian company. Hence, capital gains tax liability would not be attracted in the hands of SS(P) Ltd., the demerged company, in this case, since RV(P) Ltd. is an Indian company

- **(ii)** There would be no capital gains liability in the hands of Mr. N.K. on receipt of shares of RVP Ltd., since as per section 47(vid), any issue of shares by resulting company in a scheme of demerger to the shareholders of the demerged company will not be regarded as "transfer" for levy of capital gains tax, if issue is made in consideration of demerger of the undertaking.

- **(iii)** Yes, capital gains would arise in the hands of Mr. N.K. on sale of shares of RV(P) Ltd.

| Sale consideration | 8,00,000 |
| Less: Cost of acquisition of shares of RV(P) Ltd. (See Note) | 1,50,000 |
| Long-term capital gain (since period of holding of shares in demerged| | 6,50,000 |
| company is also to be considered) | |

Note: Cost of acquisition of shares of RV(P) Ltd.

as per section 49(2C): Cost of acquisition of Net book value of assets transferred in a demerger x shares of SS(P) Ltd. Net worth of the demerged company immediately before demerger 10 crore ₹ 6,00,000 x—_——— ₹ ₹ 1,50,000 40 crore

- **(iv)** No, sale of shares by Mr. N.K. would not affect the tax benefits availed by SS(P) Ltd. or RV(P) Ltd. There is no stipulation that they continue to remain shareholders for any period of time thereafter.

- **(v)** Since the resultant capital gain on sale of shares of RV(P) Ltd. is a long-term capital gain (on account of the period of holding of shares in demerged company being considered by virtue of section 2(42A)(g), Mr. N.K. can avail exemption under section 54F by investing the entire net consideration in purchase (within one year before and two years after the date of transfer) or construction (within three years after the date of transfer) of one residential house in India. If part of the net consideration is invested, only proportionate exemption would be available.

questions.question_title: Section 45(1A) & Section 50: Insurance Compensation for Destruction of Depreciable Capital Assets
questions.question_text:
The assessee was a company carrying on business of manufacture and sale of art-silk cloth. It purchased machinery worth ₹ 4 lacs on 1.5.2021 and insured it with United India Assurance Ltd against fire, flood, earthquake etc., The written down value of the asset as on 01.04.2025 was ₹ 1,87,850. The insurance policy contained a reinstatement clause requiring the insurance company to pay the value of the machinery, as on the date of fire etc., in case of destruction of loss. A fire broke out in August, 2025 causing extensive damage to the machinery of the assessee rendering them totally useless. The assessee company received a sum of ₹ 4 lacs from the insurance company on 15th March, 2026.

Discuss the issues arising on account on the transactions and their tax treatment.
questions.answer_text:
As per section 45(1A), where any person receives any money or other assets under an insurance from an insurer on account of damage to or destruction of capital asset as a result of, inter alia, accidental fire then, any profits and gains arising from the receipt of such money or other assets, shall be chargeable to income tax under the head "Capital Gains" and shall be deemed to be the income of such person of the previous year in which such money or asset was received.

For the purpose of section 48, the money received or the market value of the asset shall be deemed to be the full value of the consideration accruing as a result of the transfer of such capital asset.

Since the asset was destroyed and the money from the insurance company was received in the previous year, there will be a liability to capital gains in respect of insurance moneys received by the assessee.

Under section 45(1A) any profits and gains arising from receipt of insurance moneys is chargeable under the head "Capital gains".

For the purpose of section 48, the moneys received shall be deemed to be the full value of the consideration accruing or arising.

questions.question_title: Taxation on Liquidation of Company: Deemed Dividend u/s 2(22)(c), Shareholder Capital Gains u/s 46(2) & Exemption Limits u/s 54EC
questions.question_text:
Aries Tubes Private Ltd. went into liquidation on 01.12.2025. The company was seized and possessed of the following funds prior to the distribution of assets to the shareholders: 4 Share Capital (issued on 01.04.2013) 5,00,000 Reserves prior to 1.12.2025 3,00,000 Excess realization in the course of liquidation 5,00,000 Total 13,00,000 There are 5 shareholders, each of whom received ₹ 2,60,000 from the liquidator in full settlement. The shareholders desire to invest the resultant element of capital gain in long term specified assets as defined in section 54EC.

You are required to examine the various issues and advice the shareholders about their liability to income tax.
questions.answer_text:
Under section 46(1), where assets of a company are distributed to its shareholders on its liquidation, such distribution shall not be regarded as transfer in hands of the company for purpose of section 45. However, under section 46(2), where the shareholder, on liquidation of a company, receives any money or other assets from the company, he shall be chargeable to income-tax under the head "capital gains", in respect of the money so received or the market value of the other assets on the date of distribution as reduced by the amount of dividend deemed under section 2(22)(c) and the sum so arrived at shall be deemed to be the full value of the consideration for the purposes of section 48.

As per section 2(22)(c), dividend includes any distribution made to the shareholders of a company on its liquidation, to the extent to which the distribution is attributable to the accumulated profits of the company immediately before its liquidation, whether capitalized or not.

In this case, the accumulated profits immediately before liquidation is ₹ 3,00,000. The share of each shareholder is ₹ 60,000 (being one-fifth of ₹ 3,00,000). An amount of ₹ 60,000 is the deemed dividend under section 2(22)(c). The same is taxable in the hands of the shareholder under the head "Income from other sources".

Therefore, ₹ 2,00,000 [i.e. ₹ 2,60,000 minus ₹ 60,000, being deemed dividend u/s 2(22)(c)] is the full value of consideration in the hands of each shareholder as per section 46(2). Against this, investment of ₹ 1,00,000 by each shareholder is to be deducted to arrive at the capital gains of ₹ 1,00,000 of each shareholder.

Since the shares are held for more than 24 months, hence long- term capital asset.

Since the equity shares are not listed, it would not be liable for securities transaction tax and hence, capital gain (long term) would be taxable under section 112. Hence, such long term capital gain would be taxable @12.5%. —S ee Exemption under section 54EC is available only where there is an actual transfer of capital assets and not in case of deemed capital gain as per decision rendered in case of CIT v. Ruby Trading Co (P) Ltd

- **(2003)** 259 ITR 54 (Raj).

Therefore, exemption under section 54EC will not be available in this case since it is deemed transfer and not actual transfer. Furthermore, exemption under section 54EC is available only on transfer of long-term capital asset, being land or building or both. Slump Sale

questions.question_title: Section 54: Exemption for Purchase of Integrated Adjacent Flats as One Residential House
questions.question_text:
Mr. Ganesh sold his residential house in Mumbai and earned long term capital gain of 2.5 crores. He purchased two residential flats adjacent to each other on the same day vide two separate registered sale deeds from two different persons. The builder had certified that he had effected necessary modification to make it one residential apartment. Mr. Ganesh sought exemption under section 54 in respect of the investment made in purchase of the two residential flats. The Assessing Officer, however, gave exemption under section 54 to the extent of purchase of one residential flat only contending that since the long term capital gain exceeds ₹ 2 crore, sub-section (1) of section 54 clearly restricts the benefit of exemption to purchase one residential house only and the two flats cannot be treated as one residential unit since -

- **(i)** the flats were purchased through different sale deeds; and

- **(ii)** it was found by the Inspector that, before its sale to the assessee, the residential flats were in occupation of two different tenants.

Examine the correctness of the contention of the Assessing Officer.
questions.answer_text:
This issue came up before the Karnataka High Court in CIT v. D. Ananda Basappa (2009) 309 ITR 329. The Court observed that the assessee had shown that the flats were situated side by side and the builder had also certified that he had effected modification of the flats to make them one unit by opening the door between the apartments.

Therefore, it was immaterial that the flats were occupied by two different tenants prior to sale or that it was purchased through different sale deeds. The Court observed that these were not the grounds to hold that the assessee did not have the intention to purchase the two flats as one unit. The Court held that the assessee was entitled to exemption under section 54 in respect of purchase of both the flats to form one residential house. Applying the ratio of the above decision to the case on hand, Mr. Ganesh is entitled to exemption under section 54 in respect of purchase of two flats to form one residential house.

Therefore, the contention of the Assessing Officer is not correct. SSS a a a a a

questions.question_text:
Gama Ltd, located within the corporation limits decided in December, 2025 decided to shift its industrial undertaking to non-urban area. The company sold some of the assets and acquired new assets in the process of shifting. The relevant details are as follows: (% in lacs)

| Particulars | ₹ |
| :--- | :---: |
| Land | |
| Building| Plant & | Furniture | |

(Long Term) Machinery

- **(i)** | Sale proceeds (sale effected in March, 2026) 8 18 16 3

- **(ii)** | Cost of acquisition 4 10 12 2

- **(iii)** | WDV in terms of section 50 -- 4 5 2

- **(iv)** | Cost of new assets purchased in July, 2026 for the purpose of business in the new place 4 7 17 2 Compute the capital gains of Gama Ltd for the assessment year 2026-27.
questions.answer_text:
Section 54G deals with deduction in respect of any capital gain that may arise from the transfer of an industrial undertaking situated in an urban area in the course of or in consequence of shifting to a non-urban area. If the assessee purchases new machinery or plant or acquires a building or land or constructs a new building or shifts the original asset and transfers the establishment to the new area, within 1 year before or 3 years after the date on which the transfer takes place, then, instead of the capital gain being charged to tax, it shall be dealt with as under: 1. If the capital gain is greater than the cost of the new asset, the difference between the capital gain and the cost of the new asset shall be chargeable as income "under section 45". 2. Ifthe capital gain is equal to or less than the cost of the new asset, section 45 is not to be applied. The capital assets referred to in section 54G are machinery or plant or land or building or any rights in building or land. Capital gain arising on transfer of furniture does not qualify for exemption under section 54G. No exemption is therefore available under section 54G in respect of investment of ₹ 2 lacs in acquiring furniture. The first step therefore is to determine the capital gain arising out of the transfer and thereafter apply the provisions of section 54G.

- **(a)** | Land - Sale proceeds (Non-depreciable asset) 8,00,000 Less: Cost of acquisition 4,00,000 Long term capital gain 4,00,000 Less: Cost of new assets purchased within three year after the date of transfer (under section 54G) (See Note below) 3,00,000 Taxable Long term capital gain 1,00,000

- **(b)** | Building - sale proceeds (depreciable assets) 18,00,000 Less: W.D.V. is deemed as cost of acquisition under section 50 4,00,000 Short term capital gain 14,00,000

- **(c)** | Plant & machinery- sale proceeds (depreciable asset) 16,00,000 Less: WDV is deemed cost under section 50 5,00,000 Short term capital gain 11,00,000

- **(d)** | Furniture - sale proceeds (depreciable asset) 3,00,000 Less: WDV is deemed cost under section 50 2,00,000 Short term capital gain (A) 1,00,000 Summary q Short term capital gain: Building 14,00,000 Short term capital gain; Plant & machinery 11,00,000 25,00,000 Less: Section 54G [New assets purchased] (See Note below) 25,00,000 Net short term capital gain (B) Nil Total short term capital gain (A)+(B) = ₹ 1 lac Note - Total exemption available under section 54G is ₹ 28 lacs (₹ 4 lacs + ₹ 7 lacs + 7 17 lacs). The exemption should first be exhausted against short term capital gain as the incidence of tax in case of short-term capital gain is more than in case of long term capital gain.

Therefore, ₹ 25 lacs is exhausted against short term capital gain and the balance of 3 lacs against long term capital gain. The taxable capital gains would be: Long term ₹ 1,00,000 (taxable @12.5% under section 112) Short term capital gains (furniture) 3₹ 1,00,000 (taxable at applicable tax rates) 22,00,000 Tax on Capital Gain (Section 112A & 112)

provisions.topic_title: Section 4: Diversion of Income vs Application of Income
provisions.provision_presentation_markdown:
# Section 4: Diversion of Income vs. Application of Income

Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, tax is levied on the **total income** of an assessee. Understanding whether a sum represents **Diversion of Income by Overriding Title** or **Application of Income** is crucial for determining tax liability.

---

## ⚖️ Judicial Foundation: CIT v. Sitaldas Tirathdas (1961) 41 ITR 367 (SC)

The Supreme Court established the cardinal legal test to differentiate between the two concepts:

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **The True Legal Test**
> * **Diversion of Income:** Is the amount diverted *before* it reaches the assessee by an obligation created by an overriding legal title?
> * **Application of Income:** Does the amount reach the assessee first as income, and is then applied to discharge an obligation created by the assessee's own voluntary act or subsequent agreement?

---

## 📊 Comparative Analysis Matrix

| Feature / Benchmark | Diversion of Income by Overriding Title | Application of Income |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Stage of Interception** | Intercepted **before** reaching the assessee (at source). | Reaches the assessee first or accrues to them. |
| **Nature of Obligation** | Legal obligation created by superior title or statute. | Voluntary obligation or self-imposed obligation. |
| **Taxability** | **NOT Taxable** in the hands of the recipient/assessee. | **FULLY TAXABLE** in the hands of the assessee. |
| **Title to Income** | Assessee never gets a title to the income. | Assessee gets clear legal title to the income first. |
| **Example** | Sub-partnership sharing profit by statutory deed; Court decree charging property revenue for alimony. | Paying alimony out of general salary; setting aside fees for voluntary trust created by advocate. |

---

> [!WARNING]
> **Common Professional Exam Trap**
> An advocate/professional agreeing to accept fees only on condition that the client pays it into a trust *created by the advocate himself* is **NOT** a case of diversion by overriding title. The client did not create the charge or obligation prior to the fee structure; the obligation was created by the professional's own voluntary act.

provisions.topic_title: Section 4: Diversion of Income by Overriding Title vs. Application of Income
provisions.provision_presentation_markdown:
# Diversion of Income by Overriding Title vs. Application of Income

Under **Section 4 of the Income-tax Act, 1961**, tax is charged on the total income of an assessee. A fundamental judicial doctrine determines whether a particular flow of funds constitutes taxable income in the hands of the recipient or if it was diverted at source by a paramount title.

---

## 1. The Core Legal Test (*CIT v. Sitaldas Tirathdas* [1961] 41 ITR 367 SC)

The Supreme Court laid down the golden rule to distinguish between Diversion and Application:

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **The Supreme Court Test:**  
> - **Diversion by Overriding Title:** Is the amount diverted *before* it reaches the assessee? Does the obligation create an enforceable charge on the *source of income* itself?
> - **Application of Income:** Does the income reach the assessee *first*, with the assessee subsequently applying it to discharge an obligation (voluntary or contractual)?

---

## 2. Comparative Distinction Matrix

| Criteria | Diversion of Income by Overriding Title | Application of Income |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Point of Legal Obligation** | Attaches **prior** to the accrual/receipt of income at the source itself. | Attaches **after** the income has accrued to or been received by the assessee. |
| **Flow of Income** | Income is diverted to a third party before reaching the assessee. | Income reaches the assessee's hands first and is then disbursed. |
| **Taxability** | **Not taxable** in the hands of the assessee (deductible/excluded from total income). | **Fully taxable** in the hands of the assessee. |
| **Nature of Charge** | Enforceable legal charge created on the asset or source of income. | Personal obligation or contract-based payment out of earned profits. |

---

## 3. Business Takeover with Overriding Charge (*Jit & Pal X-Rays (P.) Ltd. v. CIT*)

When an assessee-company acquires a going concern subject to a pre-existing or integrated covenant charging net profits:

1. **Integration in Covenant:** If the payment obligation (e.g., annuity/overriding charge to the vendor's spouse) is embedded as an **integral condition** of the sale deed for acquiring the business asset.
2. **Charge on Source:** The obligation attaches to the very source of income (the undertaking acquired).
3. **Legal Effect:** The payment constitutes a **diversion of income by overriding title** because the assessee never acquired the right to that portion of the income.

> [!NOTE]
> **Judicial Ratio (Jit & Pal X-Rays (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2004] 267 ITR 370 (All)):**  
> Where an overriding charge of ₹ 15,000 p.a. in favour of the sole-proprietor's wife was an integral part of the sale deed transferring the going concern to XYZ Ltd. and charged on net profits, XYZ Ltd. accepted it as a condition of purchase. Hence, the obligation attached to the source, making it a **diversion of income** and not a mere application.

---

## 4. Common Exam Traps & Pitfalls

> [!WARNING]
> **Watch out for these nuances in CA Final problems:**
> - **Subsequent Voluntary Charge:** If the business is purchased first without any charge, and *later* the company voluntarily agrees to pay an amount to the vendor's family out of profits, it is **Application of Income**.
> - **Charge on Net Profits vs. Allocation of Profits:** A charge embedded in the title deed before income accrues = Diversion. Allocating net profits after annual audit = Application.
> - **Personal Debt Satisfaction:** Paying personal debts using business income is an **Application of Income**, even if bound by contract.

provisions.provision_presentation_markdown:
# Statutory Doctrine: Diversion of Income vs. Application of Income Under **Section 4 of the Income-tax Act, 1961**, income tax is charged on the total income of the assessee. A fundamental distinction developed through judicial precedents is whether an amount paid out by an assessee represents a **Diversion of Income by Overriding Title** or merely an **Application of Income**. --- ## ⚖️ The Two Pillars of Judicial Doctrine ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ INCOME GENERATED / ACCRUING FROM SOURCE │ └──────────────────────┬────────────────────────┘ │ ┌────────────────────────────────┴────────────────────────────────┐ ▼ ▼ ┌───────────────────────────────────────────┐ ┌───────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ DIVERSION BY OVERRIDING TITLE │ │ APPLICATION OF INCOME │ ├───────────────────────────────────────────┤ ├───────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ • Charge created BEFORE reaching assessee │ │ • Income reaches/accrues to assessee first│ │ • Assessee is a mere conduit/agent │ │ • Spent/applied due to voluntary/contract │ │ • EXCLUDED from Assessee's Total Income │ │ • INCLUDED in Assessee's Total Income │ └───────────────────────────────────────────┘ └───────────────────────────────────────────┘ --- ## 🔍 Comparative Landmark Matrix | Feature | Diversion of Income by Overriding Title | Application of Income | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Stage of Interception** | Prior to accrual or receipt by the assessee (At Source). | After income has accrued to or been received by the assessee. | | **Nature of Obligation** | Legal obligation that creates a paramount/superior charge over the income. | Voluntary obligation, personal debt, or contractual agreement after receipt. | | **Title to Income** | Third party possesses a superior/overriding legal title to the income. | Assessee possesses full legal title to the income before spending it. | | **Tax Treatment** | **Excluded** from total income (Not taxable in assessee's hands). | **Included** in total income (Taxable in assessee's hands). | | **Landmark Landmark Cases** | *CIT v. Sitaldas Tirathdas* (1961) 41 ITR 367 (SC)
*CIT v. Nariman B. Bharucha & Sons* (1981) 130 ITR 863 (Bom) | *Provat Kumar Mitter v. CIT* (1961) 41 ITR 624 (SC) | --- ## 🔑 Key Judicial Tests (Supreme Court - *CIT v. Sitaldas Tirathdas*) > [!IMPORTANT] > **The Benchmark Test:** > Is the amount sought to be deducted an obligation to apply income which has accrued and has been received by the assessee, OR is it an obligation to divert the income before it reaches the assessee? > > - **If the source is burdened with an obligation:** The income is diverted at source. > - **If the obligation is to apply income after receipt:** It is an application of income. --- ## 🏢 Partnership Deed Provisions & Legal Impact > [!NOTE] > **Partnership reconstituted upon death of a partner:** > If a partnership deed specifically covenants that upon the demise of a partner, the surviving partners can continue the business **only subject to a mandatory payment of a % of profits** to the deceased partner's widow/dependants, a legal charge is created directly on the firm's income generation. * **Result:** The firm receives that portion of income **for and on behalf of the beneficiary** (mother/widow). * **Tax Effect:** The amount paid is **diverted at source** by overriding title and stands **excluded** from the taxable income of the reconstituted firm. > [!WARNING] > **Common Trap in Exams:** > If the payment to a relative is purely voluntary or based on a personal maintenance agreement entered into *after* receiving profits (not embedded as a legal condition precedent in the document giving birth/continuation to the firm), it is **Application of Income** and **NO deduction/exclusion** is permissible.

# Progressive Tax Slabs under the Old Tax Regime (Opt-out of Sec 115BAC)

Under **Section 115BAC(6)** of the Income-tax Act, 1961, an assessee can opt out of the default tax regime and pay tax under the normal provisions of the Act (Old Tax Regime) as per the rates prescribed by the relevant Finance Act.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Age Criteria for Higher Basic Exemption Limit (BEL):**
> The enhanced Basic Exemption Limits of ₹ 3,00,000 and ₹ 5,00,000 are available **ONLY** to **Resident Individuals**. A Non-Resident Individual, regardless of age, gets a Basic Exemption Limit of only ₹ 2,50,000.

---

### 📊 Comparative Slab Structure (Assessment Year 2026-27)

| Total Income Slabs | Individual < 60 Years / Non-Resident | Resident Senior Citizen (Age 60 to 79 Years) | Resident Super Senior Citizen (Age 80 Years or Above) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Up to ₹ 2,50,000** | **NIL** | **NIL** | **NIL** |
| **₹ 2,50,001 – ₹ 3,00,000** | 5% | **NIL** | **NIL** |
| **₹ 3,00,001 – ₹ 5,00,000** | 5% | 5% | **NIL** |
| **₹ 5,00,001 – ₹ 10,00,000** | 20% | 20% | 20% |
| **Above ₹ 10,00,000** | 30% | 30% | 30% |

---

### ⚖️ Mandatory Statutory Additions

> [!NOTE]
> 1. **Health & Education Cess (HEC):** Mandatory @ **4%** on the aggregate of Income Tax and Surcharge (if applicable).
> 2. **Age Determination Rule:** An individual attaining the age of 60 or 80 on **1st April** of the relevant Assessment Year is deemed to have attained that age in the previous year (CBDC Circular No. 28/2016).

> [!WARNING]
> **Common Trap:** Do not apply rebate u/s 87A under the Old Tax Regime if total income exceeds ₹ 5,00,000. Under the Old Tax Regime, Section 87A rebate is capped at ₹ 12,500 for total income up to ₹ 5,00,000 only.

provisions.provision_presentation_markdown:
# Statutory Architecture: Old Tax Regime Slabs & Section 87A Rebate

Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, Section 115BAC is the default tax regime. However, an assessee can exercise an option under **Section 115BAC(6)** to shift out of the default tax regime and be taxed under the **Normal Tax Provisions (Old Tax Regime)**.

---

## 1. Normal Slab Rates for Resident Individuals (< 60 Years)

For an individual resident in India who is below the age of 60 years at any time during the previous year, tax is computed on total income using progressive slab rates:

| Total Income Slab | Tax Rate | Notes / Cumulative Tax |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Up to ₹ 2,50,000** | **NIL** | Basic Exemption Limit (BEL) |
| **₹ 2,50,001 to ₹ 5,00,000** | **5%** | Max tax in this slab: ₹ 12,500 |
| **₹ 5,00,001 to ₹ 10,00,000** | **20%** | Max tax in this slab: ₹ 1,00,000 |
| **Above ₹ 10,00,000** | **30%** | Tax @ 30% on amount exceeding ₹ 10,00,000 |

> [!NOTE]
> Higher Basic Exemption Limits apply under the Old Regime for Senior Citizens (age 60–79: **₹ 3,00,000**) and Super Senior Citizens (age 80+: **₹ 5,00,000**).

---

## 2. Statutory Rebate under Section 87A (Old Regime)

Section 87A provides tax relief to low-income resident individuals to reduce their tax burden to Nil.


Eligibility Criteria:
  ├── Assessee Status : Resident Individual ONLY (Non-Residents & Non-Individuals NOT eligible)
  ├── Income Limit    : Total Income ≤ ₹ 5,00,000 (after all Chapter VI-A deductions)
  └── Quantum of Relief: Lower of:
                          (a) 100% of Income-tax payable, OR
                          (b) ₹ 12,500


> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Difference in Section 87A between Regimes:**
> - **Old Regime u/s 87A:** Total Income limit is **₹ 5,00,000**; Max Rebate is **₹ 12,500**.
> - **New Regime u/s 115BAC:** Total Income limit is **₹ 7,00,000**; Max Rebate is **₹ 25,00,000** (plus marginal rebate for income slightly exceeding ₹ 7 Lakhs).

---

## 3. Mandatory Exclusions & Statutory Restrictions

> [!WARNING]
> **LTCG u/s 112A Exclusion:**
> Income-tax calculated on Long-Term Capital Gains under **Section 112A** (LTCG on listed equity shares/units exceeding ₹ 1,25,000) is **NOT** eligible for rebate under Section 87A. Rebate can only be adjusted against tax on other income.

# Section 115BAC: Default Tax Regime (A.Y. 2026-27)

Under sub-section (1A) of Section 115BAC, the default regime applies to Individuals, HUFs, AOPs (other than co-operative societies), BOIs, and Artificial Juridical Persons.

---

### 1. Progressive Tax Slabs Structure (A.Y. 2026-27)

| Total Income Slab (₹) | Applicable Tax Rate |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Up to ₹ 4,00,000** | **Nil** |
| **₹ 4,00,001 – ₹ 8,00,000** | **5%** |
| **₹ 8,00,001 – ₹ 12,00,000** | **10%** |
| **₹ 12,00,001 – ₹ 16,00,000** | **15%** |
| **₹ 16,00,001 – ₹ 20,00,000** | **20%** |
| **₹ 20,00,001 – ₹ 24,00,000** | **25%** |
| **Above ₹ 24,00,000** | **30%** |

---

### 2. Mandatory Add-ons & Adjustments

- **Health and Education Cess**: Charged **@ 4%** on total income tax calculated before cess.
- **Rebate u/s 87A**: Available for resident individuals with total income up to threshold limits under the new regime.
- **Surcharge**: Applicable at tiered rates (subject to maximum cap of 25% under u/s 115BAC).

> [!NOTE]
> **Default Regime Applicability**: Assessees with non-business income can choose between the Default Regime (u/s 115BAC) and the Old Regime on a year-to-year basis at the time of filing the Return of Income u/s 139(1).

> [!WARNING]
> **Disallowed Deductions**: Most Chapter VI-A deductions (like 80C, 80D, 80TTA) and specific allowances are NOT permissible under Section 115BAC unless explicitly exempted (e.g., Sec 80CCD(2) employer contribution).

# Section 115BAC: Default Tax Regime & Section 87A Rebate (A.Y. 2026-27)

### 1. Statutory Framework & Applicability
Section 115BAC acts as the **default tax regime** for Individuals, HUFs, AOPs (other than co-operative societies), BOIs, and Artificial Juridical Persons.

> [!NOTE]
> Assessees have the option to opt out of the default regime and pay tax under the normal provisions (old tax regime) by fulfilling prescribed conditions u/s 115BAC(6).

---

### 2. Revised Tax Slabs u/s 115BAC (A.Y. 2026-27)

| Total Income Slab (₹) | Rate of Tax |
| :--- | :--- |
| Up to ₹ 4,00,000 | **Nil** |
| ₹ 4,00,001 to ₹ 8,00,000 | **5%** |
| ₹ 8,00,001 to ₹ 12,00,000 | **10%** |
| ₹ 12,00,001 to ₹ 16,00,000 | **15%** |
| ₹ 16,00,001 to ₹ 20,00,000 | **20%** |
| ₹ 20,00,001 to ₹ 24,00,000 | **25%** |
| Above ₹ 24,00,000 | **30%** |

---

### 3. Rebate under Section 87A (Default Regime)

> [!IMPORTANT]
> For **Resident Individuals** paying tax under Section 115BAC:
> - **Eligibility Threshold:** Total income does not exceed **₹ 12,00,000**.
> - **Maximum Rebate Amount:** 100% of tax payable or **₹ 60,00, whichever is lower**.
> - **Marginal Relief u/s 87A:** If total income slightly exceeds ₹ 12,00,000, marginal relief is available so that tax payable does not exceed the income exceeding ₹ 12,00,000.

---

### 4. Sequential Computation Ladder


   [ Total Income: ₹ 11,00,000 ]
                │
                ▼
   ┌───────────────────────────┐
   │ Tax Slab 1 (0 - 4L): Nil  │
   │ Tax Slab 2 (4L - 8L): 5%  │ ──> ₹ 20,000
   │ Tax Slab 3 (8L - 11L): 10%│ ──> ₹ 30,000
   └───────────────────────────┘
                │
                ▼
   [ Total Tax Before Rebate: ₹ 50,000 ]
                │
                ▼
   [ Less: Rebate u/s 87A: (₹ 50,000) ] (Since Total Income ≤ ₹ 12,00,000)
                │
                ▼
   [ Net Tax Liability: Nil ]


> [!WARNING]
> Rebate u/s 87A is available **ONLY to Resident Individuals**. Non-residents or HUFs/AOPs cannot claim rebate u/s 87A regardless of their income level.

provisions.topic_title: Section 87A: Rebate and Marginal Relief under Default Tax Regime (Section 115BAC)
provisions.provision_presentation_markdown:
### Statutory Framework: Section 87A Rebate & Marginal Relief u/s 115BAC

Under the **Default Tax Regime of Section 115BAC(1A)**, resident individuals are entitled to tax relief under **Section 87A** to prevent an anomalous situation where an incremental increase in income leads to a disproportionately higher tax liability (the "cliff effect").

---

### 1. The Statutory Rule of Marginal Relief
Where the total income of a resident individual exceeds the statutory threshold up to which tax is fully rebatable, **Marginal Relief under Section 87A** ensures that:

$$\text{Tax Payable (before cess)} \le (\text{Total Income} - \text{Rebate Threshold})$$

If the normal tax computed on total income exceeds the incremental income earned above the threshold, the excess tax is granted as a rebate under Section 87A.

---

### 2. The Sequential Computation Ladder

| Step | Operation | Formula / Benchmark |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Step 1** | **Compute Incremental Income (A)** | $\text{Total Income} - \text{Threshold Limit}$ |
| **Step 2** | **Compute Baseline Tax (B)** | Tax on Total Income under Section 115BAC(1A) slab rates |
| **Step 3** | **Evaluate Marginal Inequity** | Compare **(B)** and **(A)**. If $\mathbf{B > A}$, Marginal Inequity exists |
| **Step 4** | **Rebate u/s 87A** | $\text{Rebate} = \mathbf{B - A}$ |
| **Step 5** | **Net Tax before Cess** | $\mathbf{B} - \text{Rebate} = \mathbf{A}$ (Income in excess of threshold) |
| **Step 6** | **Final Tax Liability** | $\text{Net Tax} + \text{Health & Education Cess @ 4\%}$ |

---

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Status Requirement:** Rebate and marginal relief under Section 87A are available **exclusively to resident individuals**. Non-residents (NRs), HUFs, AOPs, and BOIs cannot claim relief under Section 87A regardless of their total income level.

> [!WARNING]
> **Health & Education Cess Sequence:** Health and Education Cess @ 4% is applied **strictly after** deducting the marginal relief rebate under Section 87A. It is NEVER computed on the gross tax before rebate.

provisions.topic_title: Marginal Relief for Domestic Companies
provisions.provision_presentation_markdown:
# Marginal Relief for Domestic Companies (A.Y. 2026-27)

## 1. Domestic Company Income-tax Rates Matrix

For Assessment Year 2026-27, the normal income-tax rates for a domestic company depend on its gross receipts / turnover in **P.Y. 2023-24**:

| Assessment Year | Turnover / Gross Receipts Condition | Tax Rate |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **A.Y. 2026-27** | Gross receipts in P.Y. 2023-24 $\le$ ₹ 400 Crore | **25%** |
| **A.Y. 2026-27** | Gross receipts in P.Y. 2023-24 $>$ ₹ 400 Crore | **30%** |
| **Concessional Regimes** | Opted u/s 115BAA / 115BAB | **22% / 15%** (Flat Surcharge @ 10%) |

---

## 2. Surcharge Structure (Normal Tax Regime)

Surcharge is levied on the base tax amount based on Total Income thresholds:


                    ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
                    │                   TOTAL INCOME LEVEL                   │
                    └───────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┘
                                                │
          ┌─────────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────┐
          ▼                                     ▼                                     ▼
    Up to ₹ 1 Crore                 Exceeds ₹ 1 Cr up to ₹ 10 Cr               Exceeds ₹ 10 Crore
       [ Nil ]                                   [ 7% ]                                 [ 12% ]


---

## 3. Statutory Mechanism of Marginal Relief

When total income marginally exceeds a surcharge threshold (e.g., ₹ 1 Crore or ₹ 10 Crore), the sudden spike in surcharge can cause the **extra tax payable** to exceed the **extra income earned**.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **The Statutory Ceiling Rule:**
> Tax Payable (including Surcharge) on Total Income cannot exceed:
> $$
> \text{Tax on Threshold Limit (₹ 1 Cr / ₹ 10 Cr)} + (\text{Total Income} - \text{Threshold Limit})
> $$

### Step-by-Step Computational Ladder

1. **Step 1:** Calculate Base Tax + Surcharge on actual Total Income (**A**).
2. **Step 2:** Calculate Base Tax on exact threshold limit (e.g., ₹ 1 Crore) where surcharge rate was lower/Nil (**B**).
3. **Step 3:** Compute excess income over threshold: $\Delta Y = \text{Total Income} - \text{Threshold}$ (**C**).
4. **Step 4:** Calculate maximum permissible tax before Cess: $\text{Cap} = \mathbf{B} + \mathbf{C}$.
5. **Step 5:** **Marginal Relief** $= \mathbf{A} - \mathbf{Cap}$ (if $\mathbf{A} > \mathbf{Cap}$; else Nil).
6. **Step 6:** Net Tax Payable $= \mathbf{A} - \text{Marginal Relief}$.
7. **Step 7:** Add Health and Education Cess @ 4% on the Net Tax Payable after Marginal Relief.

> [!WARNING]
> **Common Exam Trap:**
> Health & Education Cess (4%) is applied **AFTER** deducting Marginal Relief, not before! Applying Cess prior to Marginal Relief is a frequent source of error in CA Final calculations.

provisions.topic_title: Scheme of Partial Integration of Agricultural Income
provisions.provision_presentation_markdown:
# Scheme of Partial Integration of Agricultural Income

Under Entry 82 of the Union List (List I, Seventh Schedule to the Constitution of India), Parliament has the power to tax income **other than agricultural income**. Agricultural income tax falls under Entry 46 of the State List (List II). Consequently, **Section 10(1)** of the Income-tax Act, 1961 explicitly excludes agricultural income from total income.

However, to ensure progressive tax rates on higher-income earners, the Finance Act prescribes a **Scheme of Partial Integration** for specified assessees.

---

## 1. Applicability & Eligibility Gates

Partial integration applies **only** if all three statutory conditions are satisfied:

1. **Assessee Category**: The assessee is an **Individual, HUF, AOP, BOI, or Artificial Juridical Person**. (It does **NOT** apply to Companies, Partnership Firms, LLPs, Co-operative Societies, or Local Authorities).
2. **Net Agricultural Income Gate**: Net Agricultural Income (Gross Agricultural Receipts less allowable revenue expenses u/s 10(1)) exceeds **₹ 5,000** in the Previous Year.
3. **Non-Agricultural Income Gate**: Total Non-Agricultural Income exceeds the applicable **Basic Exemption Limit (BEL)**.

> [!NOTE] Basic Exemption Limits under Optional/Old Tax Regime
> - **Individual (< 60 years)**: ₹ 2,50,000
> - **Senior Citizen Resident (60 to 79 years)**: ₹ 3,00,000
> - **Super Senior Citizen Resident (80+ years)**: ₹ 5,00,000

---

## 2. Sequential Mathematical Computation Ladder

When partial integration applies, tax liability before rebate/cess is computed using the standard 4-Step Mechanism:

| Step | Description | Formula / Action |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Step 1** | Tax on Aggregated Base | Compute income-tax on (Total Non-Agri Income + Net Agri Income) at regular slab rates. |
| **Step 2** | Tax on Ag Base + Exemption | Compute income-tax on (Net Agri Income + Basic Exemption Limit) at regular slab rates. |
| **Step 3** | Net Base Tax | Deduct Step 2 tax from Step 1 tax: **Step 3 Tax = Step 1 Tax - Step 2 Tax** |
| **Step 4** | Surcharge & Health/Edu Cess | Deduct Rebate u/s 87A (if eligible), add applicable Surcharge, and add **4% Health & Education Cess**. |

> [!IMPORTANT] Tax Effect of Partial Integration
> Step 2 ensures that agricultural income itself is not taxed. Instead, agricultural income consumes the lower tax slabs, forcing the non-agricultural income to be taxed at higher marginal slab rates (20% / 30%).

---

## 3. Comparative Matrix: Age-Wise Impact Analysis

Assuming Total Non-Agricultural Income = ₹ 7,80,000 and Net Agricultural Income = ₹ 2,90,000:

| Parameter | Age 40 Years (BEL = ₹ 2.50L) | Age 75 Years (BEL = ₹ 3.00L) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Net Agri Income** | ₹ 2,90,000 | ₹ 2,90,000 |
| **Non-Agri Total Income** | ₹ 7,80,000 | ₹ 7,80,000 |
| **Step 1: Aggregate Base** | ₹ 10,70,000 | ₹ 10,70,000 |
| **Step 1 Tax** | ₹ 1,33,500 *(12.5k + 1L + 21k)* | ₹ 1,31,000 *(10k + 1L + 21k)* |
| **Step 2: Agri + BEL Base** | ₹ 5,40,000 *(2.90L + 2.50L)* | ₹ 5,90,000 *(2.90L + 3.00L)* |
| **Step 2 Tax** | ₹ 20,500 *(12.5k + 8k)* | ₹ 28,000 *(10k + 18k)* |
| **Step 3: Basic Tax (S1 - S2)** | ₹ 1,13,000 | ₹ 1,03,000 |
| **Step 4: Tax with 4% Cess** | **₹ 1,17,520** | **₹ 1,07,120** |

> [!WARNING] Statutory Common Pitfall
> Do not deduct agricultural income expenses twice. Expenses incurred to earn agricultural income are deducted **only** while computing Net Agricultural Income. They cannot be set off against Non-Agricultural heads of income like Salary or House Property.

provisions.subject: dt
provisions.topic_title: Section 2(1A) & 10(1): Definition and Tests of Agricultural Income
provisions.provision_presentation_markdown:
# Statutory Provisions: Exemption of Agricultural Income u/s 10(1) r.w.s. 2(1A)

Under **Section 10(1)** of the Income-tax Act, 1961, agricultural income is completely exempt from tax. However, to qualify for exemption, the income must strictly satisfy the statutory criteria stipulated under **Section 2(1A)**.

---

## 1. Statutory Definition [Section 2(1A)]

Agricultural income means:

1. **Rent or Revenue [Sec. 2(1A)(a)]**: Any rent or revenue derived from land which is situated in India and is used for agricultural purposes.
2. **Income from Agriculture / Processing / Sale [Sec. 2(1A)(b)]**: Any income derived from such land by:
   - Agricultural operations;
   - Performance of any process ordinarily employed by a cultivator to render the produce fit to be taken to market; or
   - Sale of produce raised or received as rent in kind.
3. **Farm Building Income [Sec. 2(1A)(c)]**: Income derived from a building required as a dwelling house, storehouse, or out-building in immediate vicinity of agricultural land.

---

## 2. Fundamental Legal Test: Meaning of "Agricultural Operations"

> [!NOTE] Benchmark Precedent: CIT v. Raja Benoy Kumar Sahas Roy (1957) 32 ITR 466 (SC)
> The Supreme Court established that for income to be agricultural, it must be generated by carrying out basic agricultural operations requiring human labor and skill directly upon the land.

| Classification | Operations Included | Legal Treatment |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Basic Operations** | Tilling of land, sowing of seeds, planting, and similar operations directly on the soil requiring human labor and skill. | **Essential condition** to establish agricultural character. |
| **Subsequent Operations** | Weeding, digging around plants, pruning, harvesting, and protection from pests/pests control. | Qualifies as agricultural **only if** preceded by basic operations. |

---

## 3. Doctrine of Direct Nexus ("Derived From")

The statutory expression **"derived from land"** implies that the land must be the direct, effective, and immediate source of the income, not merely an indirect or incidental location.


Land Situated in India + Used for Agricultural Purposes + Basic Operations Carried Out
                                    │
                                    ▼
                   Direct Nexus Established = Section 10(1) Exempt


> [!WARNING] Landmark Distinction: Film Shooting / Non-Agricultural Land Use
> In **B. Nagi Reddi v. CIT (2002) 258 ITR 719 (Mad HC)**, relying on the Apex Court principles, it was held that where agricultural land is let out for film shooting, the rent received is **NOT agricultural income** because:
> - The immediate source of income is the commercial contract for shooting, not agricultural activity.
> - The receipt has no nexus with basic agricultural operations or sale of produce, despite the land being agricultural land.

---

## 4. Summary Matrix: Characterization of Income Receipts

| Receipt Type | Direct Nexus with Agriculture? | Taxable Head | Statutory Status |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Rent from tenant cultivating land | Yes | Exempt u/s 10(1) | Agricultural Income |
| Sale proceed of crops grown by owner | Yes | Exempt u/s 10(1) | Agricultural Income |
| Rent for film shooting on agri land | **No** | Income from Other Sources / PGBP | **Taxable** |
| Staging exhibitions / Fairs on agri land | **No** | Income from Other Sources | **Taxable** |
| Storage fees for commercial goods | **No** | Income from Other Sources | **Taxable** |

provisions.provision_presentation_markdown:
# Statutory Framework: Agricultural Income & Special Exemptions

## 1. Farm Building Rent: Agricultural vs. Non-Agricultural Use
Under **Section 2(1A)**, income derived from a building situated on or in the immediate vicinity of agricultural land qualifies as agricultural income **only if** it is occupied by the cultivator/receiver of rent-in-kind as a dwelling house, storehouse, or out-house in connection with agricultural operations.

> [!WARNING] Explanation 2 to Section 2(1A): Non-Agricultural Purpose Disqualification
> Any income derived from any building used for **any purpose other than agriculture** (including letting out for residential purposes or for business/profession) **shall NOT be treated as agricultural income**.

### Characterization Matrix

| Tenant / Occupant Type | Usage Purpose | Tax Treatment under Income-tax Act | Statutory Basis |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Agricultural Labourer / Cultivator | Residence / Farm Operations | Exempt Agricultural Income u/s 10(1) | Section 2(1A)(c) |
| Industrial Workers / Non-Agriculturists | Residential Accommodation | **Taxable Income** (IFOS / House Property) | Section 2(1A) Explanation 2 |
| Commercial Traders | Business / Godown / Office | **Taxable Income** | Section 2(1A) Explanation 2 |

---

## 2. Nursery Income & Seedlings Rule
Prior to statutory clarification, nursery income required proof of basic operations on land (tilling, sowing, planting) to qualify as agricultural income.

> [!NOTE] Explanation 3 to Section 2(1A): Deemed Agricultural Income
> Income derived from **saplings or seedlings grown in a nursery** shall be deemed to be agricultural income, **whether or not the basic operations were carried out on land**.

- **Impact:** Nursery operators are not required to prove tilling or soil preparation. Income from sale of nursery plants/seedlings is fully exempt under **Section 10(1)**.

---

## 3. Special Tax Exemption for Sikkimese Individuals
Under **Section 10(26AAA)**, specific incomes of a Sikkimese individual are completely excluded from Total Income.

> [!IMPORTANT] Scope of Section 10(26AAA) Exemption
> Income accruing or arising to a **Sikkimese individual** from:
> 1. Any source in the **State of Sikkim**; OR
> 2. Income by way of **dividend or interest on securities** (from any part of India).

### Scope of Exemption

| Nature of Income | Source Location | Taxability u/s 10(26AAA) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Business Net Profit | Located within Sikkim | **Fully Exempt** |
| Interest on Govt Securities / Bonds | Anywhere in India (e.g. Rajasthan Govt) | **Fully Exempt** |
| Dividend Income | Indian Companies | **Fully Exempt** |
| Salary / Business Income | Outside Sikkim (e.g. Mumbai / Delhi) | **Taxable** |

provisions.topic_title: Section 10(10BC): Exemption of Disaster Compensation
provisions.provision_presentation_markdown:
# Section 10(10BC): Exemption for Compensation Received on Account of Disaster

## 1. Statutory Exemption Framework

Under **Section 10(10BC)** of the Income-tax Act, 1961, compensation paid to an individual or their legal heir due to a disaster is excluded from total income subject to specific statutory conditions.

| Statutory Criteria | Statutory Requirement / Definition |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Eligible Payers** | Central Government, State Government, or a Local Authority |
| **Eligible Recipients** | The affected Individual or their Legal Heir(s) |
| **Tax Status** | Fully Exempt from Income Tax |
| **Non-Eligible Payers** | Private companies, trusts, or non-governmental entities (unless backed by Government funds) |

> [!NOTE] Statutory Intent: Tax-Free Relief
> The objective of Section 10(10BC) is humanitarian—ensuring that state-funded relief provided to victims or surviving family members during catastrophic events is not diminished by income taxation.

---

## 2. Definition of 'Disaster'

Section 10(10BC) explicitly imports the definition of **'Disaster'** from **Section 2(d) of the Disaster Management Act, 2005**.

> [!IMPORTANT] Definition of Disaster u/s 2(d) of Disaster Management Act, 2005
> Disaster means a **catastrophe, mishap, calamity or grave occurrence** in any area, arising from **natural or man-made causes**, or by **accident or negligence**, which results in:
> 1. Substantial loss of life or human suffering; OR
> 2. Damage to, and destruction of, property; OR
> 3. Damage to, or degradation of, environment;
> 
> And is of such a nature or magnitude to be **beyond the coping capacity** of the community of the affected area.

### Breakdown of Key Elements:
- **Causes**: Covers both Natural (e.g., floods, earthquakes) and Man-Made (e.g., bomb blasts, terror attacks, riots, industrial accidents).
- **Impact**: Requires substantial human loss/suffering or massive property destruction.
- **Threshold**: Must exceed the coping capacity of the affected local community.

---

## 3. Statutory Carve-Out (Proviso - Restriction on Double Benefit)

> [!WARNING] Restriction on Double Benefit (Proviso to Sec 10(10BC))
> Exemption under Section 10(10BC) shall **NOT** apply to the extent that any amount received/receivable has already been allowed as a **deduction** under the Income-tax Act on account of any loss or damage caused by such disaster.

* **Example**: If a business trader claims a loss of stock due to a flood as a deductible business loss u/s 28/37, any disaster compensation received specifically offsetting that exact loss to that extent will not enjoy exemption to avoid double benefit.

provisions.topic_title: Section 47(vii): Exemption of Capital Gains on Amalgamation of Companies
provisions.provision_presentation_markdown:
# Statutory Architecture: Exemption of Capital Gains on Share Amalgamation u/s 47(vii)

Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, the transfer of a capital asset generally attracts capital gains tax under Section 45. However, specific legislative exemptions are carved out under Section 47 where certain transactions are explicitly deemed **not** to be a 'transfer'. One such vital relief is provided to shareholders during the amalgamation of companies.

> [!IMPORTANT] Core Objective of Section 47(vii): To facilitate corporate restructuring, mergers, and business combinations without imposing immediate tax friction on the shareholders of the amalgamating company.

## Statutory Conditions for Exemption u/s 47(vii)

To claim immunity from capital gains tax upon receiving shares in an amalgamated company in lieu of shares held in an amalgamating company, the following cumulative conditions must be satisfied:

| Condition Parameter | Statutory Requirement | Legal Implication |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Status of Amalgamated Company** | The amalgamated company **must be an Indian company** | Foreign-to-foreign amalgamations do not qualify for this shareholder-level exemption. |
| **Nature of Consideration** | Consideration receivable by the shareholder must consist **solely or partly of the allotment of shares** in the amalgamated company | Allotment of cash alone will forfeit the exemption under this clause. |
| **Extinguishment of Rights** | The transfer must be by way of relinquishment or extinguishment of shares in the amalgamating company | Direct consequence of the merger scheme sanctioned by competent authorities (e.g., NCLT). |

## Subsequent Tax Mechanics: Cost of Acquisition u/s 49(2)

While Section 47(vii) defers the capital gains tax at the time of amalgamation, the tax liability is not wiped out permanently. It is preserved through a cost-substitution mechanism:

> [!NOTE] Cost Substitution Rule (Section 49(2)): The cost of acquisition of the new shares allotted in the amalgamated company shall be deemed to be the cost for which the shareholder acquired the original shares in the amalgamating company.

- **Holding Period Reckoning u/s 2(42A):** For computing the period of holding of the shares in the amalgamated company, the period for which the original shares in the amalgamating company were held by the assessee must be included.
- **Market Value Fluctuations:** Any variation in the market value of shares allotted under the amalgamation scheme (whether higher or lower than the original holding value) is irrelevant for the computation of capital gains at the time of amalgamation.

provisions.topic_title: Section 47: Transactions Not Regarded as Transfer (Exempted Capital Asset Transfers)
provisions.provision_presentation_markdown:
# Section 47: Transactions Not Regarded as Transfer ## 1. Statutory Framework (Section 45 vs Section 47) Under **Section 45(1)** of the Income-tax Act, 1961, any profits or gains arising from the transfer of a capital asset effected in the previous year are chargeable to income tax under the head *Capital Gains*. However, **Section 47** enumerates specific transactions which, despite involving a change in ownership or form of capital assets, are statutory exceptions and are **not regarded as transfer** for the purpose of capital gains tax. > [!NOTE] Fundamental Legal Effect > If a transaction falls under any clause of Section 47: > - No Capital Gains tax liability arises in the hands of the transferor at the time of such transaction. > - The recipient generally takes the **Cost of Acquisition to the Previous Owner** u/s 49(1) and **tacks on the Period of Holding** u/s 2(42A) when sold subsequently. --- ## 2. Key Statutory Exemptions u/s 47 | Section Clause | Transaction Description | Taxability at the Time of Transaction | Subsequent Cost & Period of Holding to Transferee | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Section 47(i)** | Total or partial partition of a Hindu Undivided Family (HUF) where capital assets are distributed in kind to members. | **NIL** (Not a Transfer) | Cost = Cost to HUF u/s 49(1)
POH = Includes period held by HUF | | **Section 47(iii)** | Transfer of a capital asset under a **Gift** or an **Irrevocable Trust** (except ESOP shares transferred by employees). | **NIL** (Not a Transfer) | Cost = Cost to Donor u/s 49(1)
POH = Includes period held by Donor | | **Section 47(x)** | Conversion of bonds, debentures, debenture stock, or deposit certificates of a company into shares or debentures of that company. | **NIL** (Not a Transfer) | Cost = Cost of original debentures/bonds u/s 49(2A)
POH = Includes period held prior to conversion u/s 2(42A) | --- ## 3. Detailed Breakdown of Specific Statutory Exemptions ### A. Partition of HUF [Section 47(i)] - Distribution of capital assets (in kind) amongst members on total or partial partition of an HUF does not constitute a transfer. - **Rationale:** Partition is merely a mutual adjustment and division of pre-existing joint property rights among co-parceners/members, not a commercial sale or disposition. ### B. Transfers via Gift or Irrevocable Trust [Section 47(iii)] - Any transfer of a capital asset made under a gift or an irrevocable trust is excluded from the scope of transfer. - **Exception to Rule:** Transfer of shares/securities acquired under Employees Stock Option Plan (ESOP) by an employee to any person by way of gift remains subject to capital gains tax framework. > [!WARNING] Distinction between Gift & Sale > A gift must be voluntary and made without monetary or valuable consideration. If consideration is present, Section 47(iii) protection is lost. ### C. Conversion of Debentures or Bonds into Shares [Section 47(x)] - Conversion of convertible debentures, bonds, debenture-stock, or deposit certificates of a company into shares or debentures of the **same company** is exempt from capital gains. - **Tax Treatment on Subsequent Sale of Converted Shares:** - **Cost of Acquisition:** Cost of the original debentures/bonds [Section 49(2A)]. - **Period of Holding:** Includes the period for which the original debentures/bonds were held prior to conversion [Section 2(42A)(hf)].

provisions.topic_title: Tax Treatment of Reverse Mortgage Scheme u/s 47(xvi) and 10(43)
provisions.provision_presentation_markdown:
# Tax Framework for Reverse Mortgage Scheme

## Overview of Statutory Architecture

The Reverse Mortgage Scheme was introduced to provide financial security to senior citizens owning residential property. Under this scheme, senior citizens can mortgage their house with a bank/housing finance company to receive periodical payments or a lump sum, while retaining life interest in the property.

| Statutory Provision | Subject / Context | Tax Impact / Treatment |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Section 47(xvi)** | Creation of mortgage over capital asset under notified scheme | **Not a 'Transfer'**: No capital gains tax liability on mortgaging property |
| **Section 10(43)** | Receipts of loan amount (lump sum or installment) | **Exempt Income**: Excluded from Total Income of the borrower |
| **Section 45** | Subsequent alienation/sale of property by mortgagee to enforce recovery | **Taxable Event**: Capital gains triggered upon final sale/alienation |

---

## Key Legal Elements

### 1. Exclusion from Transfer [Section 47(xvi)]
- Any transfer of a capital asset in a transaction of reverse mortgage under a scheme made and notified by the Central Government **shall not be regarded as a transfer** for the purpose of capital gains under Section 45.
- **Timing of Relief**: Exemption from transfer status applies both at the time of entering into the mortgage agreement and during the currency of the mortgage tenure.

> [!NOTE] Statutory Eligibility Criteria: The reverse mortgage scheme must be specifically notified by the Central Government in the Official Gazette to qualify for benefit under Section 47(xvi).

### 2. Complete Income Exemption [Section 10(43)]
- Any amount received by an individual as a loan, whether in a **lump sum** or in **installment**, in a transaction of reverse mortgage is **totally exempt** from income tax.
- **Nature of Receipt**: Since loan receipts represent capital receipts with an obligation to repay (or adjust against asset proceeds), they do not constitute income in the hands of the borrower.

> [!IMPORTANT] No TDS Application: As the loan receipts under Section 10(43) are exempt from tax, the lending institution is not required to deduct tax at source (TDS) under any provisions of Chapter XVII-B.

### 3. Taxability upon Final Alienation / Recovery
- Capital gains tax liability is **deferred**, not completely extinguished.
- When the lender/bank enforces its security upon maturity or default by selling or alienating the mortgaged property to recover the outstanding loan and accrued interest:
  - The transaction constitutes a taxable transfer under Section 45.
  - Capital gains (Long-Term or Short-Term depending on holding period) must be computed in accordance with statutory rules.
  - Excess proceeds, if any, after adjusting the outstanding loan and recovery expenses, belong to the borrower or legal heirs.

> [!WARNING] Legal Basis of Taxability on Alienation: Capital gains arise at the point of ultimate alienation of the property by the bank, as the ownership rights are permanently transferred to a third-party purchaser.

provisions.topic_title: Section 55: Cost of Acquisition and Cost of Improvement for Pre-2001 Capital Assets
provisions.provision_presentation_markdown:
### Statutory Determination of Cost of Acquisition & Cost of Improvement (Pre-2001 Assets)

Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, special provisions apply for determining the **Cost of Acquisition (COA)** and **Cost of Improvement (COI)** when computing Capital Gains on assets acquired prior to **April 1, 2001**.

---

### 1. Cost of Acquisition (COA) u/s 55(2)(b)

Where a capital asset became the property of the assessee before **April 1, 2001**, the assessee has the option to substitute the **Fair Market Value (FMV)** as on April 1, 2001 in place of the actual cost of acquisition.

#### Formula for COA Determination:
$$\text{COA} = \max\Big(\text{Actual Acquisition Cost},\, \min(\text{FMV as on 01.04.2001},\, \text{SDV as on 01.04.2001})\Big)$$

> [!IMPORTANT] Statutory Cap on FMV for Immovable Property
> As per the proviso to Section 55(2)(b)(i), in case of **land or building (or both)**, the Fair Market Value as on April 1, 2001 **cannot exceed** the Stamp Duty Value (SDV) assessed or assessable on April 1, 2001. If SDV as on April 1, 2001 is available, FMV is capped at SDV.

---

### 2. Cost of Improvement (COI) u/s 55(1)(b)

| Period of Improvement Expenditure | Tax Treatment u/s 55(1)(b) |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Incurred Prior to April 1, 2001** | **Completely Ignored (NIL)**. Capitalized expenses prior to 01.04.2001 are deemed absorbed into the FMV as on 01.04.2001. |
| **Incurred On or After April 1, 2001** | **Fully Deductible**. Included at actual expenditure incurred by the assessee or previous owner. |

---

### 3. Order of Computation u/s 48

- **Gross Sale Consideration**
- *Less:* Expenditure incurred wholly and exclusively in connection with transfer
- **= Net Sale Consideration**
- *Less:* Cost of Acquisition (determined u/s 55(2)(b))
- *Less:* Cost of Improvement (incurred on or after 01.04.2001 u/s 55(1)(b))
- **= Taxable Capital Gain**

> [!NOTE] Key Statutory Takeaway
> Expenses incurred on addition, alteration, or reconstruction prior to April 1, 2001 can **NEVER** be claimed separately as Cost of Improvement, regardless of the nature or magnitude of the expense.
